title: Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance

concept.text: Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance would let clinicians select an antigen, or a defined set of antigens, and induce durable immune unresponsiveness to those targets while preserving protective immunity. Targets could include a patient's own proteins involved in autoimmune disease, allergens, donor antigens on transplanted tissue, or components of a therapeutic product. The intended clinical outcome is lasting control after a single treatment or short course, with freedom from chronic systemic immunosuppression.

The biological foundation is the immune system's existing capacity to restrain self-reactive lymphocytes through peripheral tolerance. Candidate therapeutic routes include antigen delivery through peptides or tolerogenic nanoparticles, engineered regulatory cells, and selective targeting of pathogenic lymphocytes. A broadly adaptable platform would need to connect a chosen target to a reliable, durable tolerizing response across clinically relevant settings. These approaches remain at different stages of development, and the supplied evidence establishes the therapeutic goal and component strategies.

significance.text: Many treatments for autoimmune disease, transplant rejection and related immune disorders rely on broadly acting immunosuppression, with associated adverse effects. Durable control focused on selected pathogenic antigens could change the relationship between disease control and immune protection. Conditional on adequate target coverage and control of the relevant immune mechanisms, it could enable drug-free control of antigen-defined autoimmune disease, durable control of severe allergy, and acceptance of allogeneic organs or cell grafts without chronic systemic immunosuppression. Preserving defenses against pathogens and cancer is central to the proposed benefit.

The same capability could address immune responses that limit therapeutic proteins and gene delivery. Relevant gene-therapy targets may include the delivery vector or the therapeutic product, while enzyme replacement can provoke immunity against the administered enzyme. Preventing new immune responses and managing established neutralizing antibodies are separate therapeutic tasks. Pre-existing antibodies against adeno-associated viruses and antibodies induced by repeated exposure illustrate why successful tolerance induction would still need to be evaluated against the patient's existing humoral immunity.

The breadth of benefit would depend on identifying and covering the antigens that actually sustain disease. Human autoimmune responses can involve multiple targets that vary between patients and disease stages. Silencing a selected response could therefore leave other pathogenic responses active. A broadly adaptable tolerance platform would need evidence across these variations before claims of general applicability became convincing.

Conditional synthesis. Successful immune control could make tissue repair, cell replacement and transplantation more durable by reducing immune-mediated damage. Established tissue destruction would still require restoration or replacement, and graft performance would continue to depend on nonimmune biological and engineering factors. Xenotransplants and immunogenic bioengineered grafts could benefit from tolerance or equivalent immune protection, alongside solutions to their other barriers.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a generalizable clinical method that reliably produces durable unresponsiveness to selected pathogenic or donor antigens while preserving protective immunity. The supplied 2023 review describes robust, long-lasting antigen-specific tolerance as an unmet clinical goal. Achieving that goal requires control of the immune cells and interactions sustaining disease, together with evidence that the resulting state persists after treatment ends.

Target identification and coverage are major barriers. Self-reactive lymphocytes can escape central tolerance and subsequently require peripheral restraint. Autoimmune disease often involves several autoantigens, with specificity changing across patients and over time. Epitope spreading can expand the response after treatment begins. The review identifies possible requirements including halting that spreading, repeatedly reassessing antigen specificity, or inducing bystander tolerance that extends suppression to nearby pathogenic responses. The breadth and selectivity of such effects would need clinical characterization.

Engineering barriers include delivering antigens in a context that reliably induces tolerance, making regulatory or selectively targeted cellular approaches effective and durable, and translating encouraging preclinical results into reproducible human outcomes. The desired selectivity also creates a measurement problem. Clinical improvement must be connected to durable control of the relevant antigen-specific response, with functional evidence that protective immunity remains effective.

Durable drug-free remission also requires mechanistic understanding and predictive biomarkers. The 2026 cellular-immunotherapy review describes uncertainty about the mechanisms and biomarkers underlying lasting remission after treatment. Existing neutralizing antibodies add a further boundary for applications involving therapeutic products or vectors, because tolerance to future stimulation alone would leave the fate of those antibodies unresolved.

current_state.text: The review published on 12 December 2023, Therapeutic induction of antigen-specific immune tolerance, describes an unmet need across autoimmunity, allergy, organ transplantation and gene therapy. It surveys peptide, nanoparticle, nucleic-acid and cell-based approaches, including encouraging preclinical results and early clinical development. At its publication date, it reported that truly antigen-specific immunotherapies had yet to receive approval for autoimmune disease or organ transplantation, and that few approaches had progressed beyond phase I or II trials. This provides a dated clinical-development assessment whose scope includes substantial experimental progress.

Clinical progress of engineered cellular immunotherapies for autoimmunity, published on 16 February 2026, summarizes clinical results made public principally through November 2025. It reports drug-free complete remission in the first eight refractory systemic lupus erythematosus cases treated with anti-CD19 CAR T cells, with SLEDAI scores of 0. Follow-up extended beyond four years in some cases, despite B-cell return after 2–7 months. The longest duration describes the maximum reported follow-up. The evidence discussed includes case series and a 58-person systematic review, leaving the durability, safety and generalizability of these outcomes to be established in broader clinical experience.

Outcomes differed across diseases in that review. Systemic sclerosis activity improved, including a median 31% improvement in modified Rodnan skin score in one series, while remission remained unreported in the cited experience. Three individuals with rheumatoid arthritis receiving anti-CD19 CAR T cells achieved drug-free DAS-28-ESR/CRP remission. The section also describes three recipients of cytokine-secreting engineered anti-CD19 cells. These small patient counts limit conclusions about reproducibility and population-wide benefit.

Anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy targets the B-cell lineage. Its remission results demonstrate clinically important immune intervention, while leaving chosen disease-antigen tolerance to be established through separate evidence. The same review discusses more selective approaches directed at antigen-specific B-cell receptors, including chimeric autoantibody receptor strategies. It also reports that some participants with type 1 diabetes achieved insulin independence in a study of regulatory T cells with or without rituximab. Insulin independence is a meaningful clinical response whose mechanism and durability require separate assessment before an antigen-specific cure can be established.

The supplied reviews establish neither a general programmable tolerance platform nor an antigen-specific cure of multiple sclerosis or type 1 diabetes. Their coverage also leaves the worldwide extent of demonstrated transplant tolerance unresolved. The supplied freshness record contains no bounded search establishing developments through 1 November 2026, so the contemporary availability or absence of the proposed general capability remains unverified.

Evidence access is described here from the supplied review and source index. The retained 2023 article extraction is partial, with truncation in the references and substantive review sections available. The 2026 article extraction is recorded as complete through references and end matter. The supplied review verified both article identities. These access details support interpretation of the retained passages while leaving the freshness gap unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. A single treatment or short course would produce years of clinically meaningful antigen-specific unresponsiveness in more than one disease class, such as an autoimmune disease and organ transplantation, without chronic systemic immunosuppression. Trials would prespecify the target antigens, treatment exposure, disease-specific clinical outcomes, permitted rescue treatment and duration of follow-up. The short-course and multi-year requirements are proposed benchmarks for this innovation.
completion_criteria.label: Years-long short-course tolerance spans disease classes without chronic immunosuppression

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Prespecified functional assays would show sustained control of pathogenic responses to the selected antigens alongside clinical benefit. Assessment would address relevant cellular responses, pathogenic antibodies where applicable, antigen coverage and epitope spreading. Preserved responses to vaccination and prospectively assessed protection against new infections would help establish selectivity. In gene or enzyme therapy, outcomes would separately assess prevention of new immunity and the persistence or removal of pre-existing neutralizing antibodies.
completion_criteria.label: Assays show sustained antigen-specific control while preserving protective immunity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement. Results would be reproduced across independent centers and appropriately characterized patient groups, with transparent reporting of failures, relapses and rescue therapy. Studies would define practical boundaries such as eligible antigen targets, variation in baseline immune responses, disease stage and the contribution of irreversible tissue damage. Success in two disease classes would establish demonstrated cross-indication breadth. Further indications and target sets would require their own evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent centers reproduce results with reported failures and applicability limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety requirement. Long-term follow-up would include a registry with a prespecified sample size, duration and statistical analysis plan addressing clinically meaningful serious-infection and malignancy signals. Investigators would report the precision and limits of risk estimates, alongside evidence about protective immunity. A finite registry can characterize risks within its observed population and follow-up period, with residual uncertainty for rare or delayed harms.
completion_criteria.label: Long-term registry quantifies serious-infection and malignancy risks with uncertainty

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. CLM-05, Durable organ xenotransplantation at clinical scale, shares the challenge of immune acceptance of donor tissue. Programmable tolerance could contribute to durable graft acceptance, while xenotransplantation also depends on species compatibility, organ function and clinical-scale delivery. Each entry retains its own completion condition.

Roster-based synthesis. CLM-11, Implantable human-scale organs assembled outside the body, overlaps where an assembled organ carries antigens that provoke recipient immunity. Tolerance could help protect such grafts. Organ construction, maturation, vascular integration and functional performance remain separate requirements, and the immune burden depends on the cells and materials used.

Roster-based synthesis. CLM-09, Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver, could benefit from control of immunity against delivery components or newly expressed therapeutic products. Genome-writing efficacy, tissue delivery and editing safety define additional capabilities. CLM-01 addresses the immune response surrounding an intervention.

Roster-based synthesis. CLM-10, Vaccines that elicit broad protection against hypervariable viruses, and CLM-02, Clearance of persistent viral reservoirs that force lifelong therapy, overlap through antigen recognition and the need for effective protective immunity. Vaccination seeks protective responses across variable viral targets, reservoir clearance seeks elimination of persistent infection, and programmable tolerance seeks durable restraint of selected harmful responses. Demonstrating preserved antiviral protection is therefore an important boundary for CLM-01.

Roster-based synthesis. CLM-07, Reproducible eradication of metastatic carcinoma, intersects with the requirement to preserve immunity against cancer. Any extension of tolerance to antigens shared with tumors would need careful functional assessment. Cancer eradication remains a separate therapeutic outcome.

Roster-based synthesis. CLM-04, Restoration of adult human central nervous system circuitry after injury, CLM-06, Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart, and CLM-15, Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney, concern recovery or replacement of damaged tissue. CLM-01 could support selected applications involving immune-mediated injury or immunogenic replacement cells. Restoration of circuitry, muscle or nephrons requires additional regenerative capabilities.

change_log.change: Preserved CLM-01 and its title, and expanded the concept into a plain-language account of selected targets, durable tolerance and candidate therapeutic routes.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent, and the research and review provide complementary biological and clinical detail.

change_log.change: Qualified claims about the present-day absence of a general platform and anchored clinical-development statements to the reviews' publication and coverage dates.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness record does not establish the field's status through November 2026.

change_log.change: Retained self-reactive escape from central tolerance and removed the corresponding blanket assertion about donor-reactive lymphocytes.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence directly supports the self-reactive mechanism and leaves the broader donor-reactive wording unsubstantiated.

change_log.change: Expanded antigen coverage, patient variation, epitope spreading and possible bystander tolerance within the engineering barriers.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why selected-antigen control may fail to cover the full pathogenic response.

change_log.change: Preserved and specified the lupus, systemic sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis findings, including patient counts, remission measures, B-cell return and maximum follow-up.
change_log.reason: The review supports these quantitative details and requires distinguishing the longest observed response from outcomes for every participant.

change_log.change: Added the reported type 1 diabetes insulin-independence finding and qualified broad negative assertions about transplantation, multiple sclerosis and type 1 diabetes.
change_log.reason: Clinical response, antigen-specific cure and the coverage of the supplied reviews require separate interpretation.

change_log.change: Explained the relationship between anti-CD19 lineage targeting, disease-antigen-directed approaches and the proposed tolerance platform.
change_log.reason: Clinical remission after B-cell depletion supplies relevant progress while leaving programmed antigen-specific unresponsiveness to be demonstrated.

change_log.change: Corrected the conflation of vector immunity with immunity to therapeutic enzymes and retained uncertainty about established neutralizing antibodies.
change_log.reason: Different therapeutic components can become immune targets, and prevention of future responses alone does not establish removal of existing antibodies.

change_log.change: Qualified downstream benefits for grafts, xenotransplantation and tissue restoration.
change_log.reason: Immune tolerance could contribute to these outcomes alongside independent biological and engineering requirements.

change_log.change: Made completion criteria explicitly proposed and added assessable endpoints, independent replication, practical boundaries and statistically planned safety surveillance.
change_log.reason: The source material supports the clinical goals without establishing consensus thresholds or guaranteeing detection of rare harms.

change_log.change: Preserved extraction limitations and identified roster-based relationships as synthesis.
change_log.reason: The final record must distinguish supplied evidence from proposed demonstrations and conceptual integration without implying new document inspection.

unresolved_issues: The availability or absence of a broadly adaptable clinical tolerance platform through 1 November 2026 remains unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.

The supplied reviews do not resolve the worldwide scope of demonstrated transplant tolerance or establish comprehensive contemporary absence claims for antigen-specific cures of multiple sclerosis and type 1 diabetes.
The antigen sets, assays and biomarkers needed to predict durable tolerance across patients, disease stages and indications remain unresolved.
The extent to which a tolerizing intervention could control established antibody-producing responses or eliminate pre-existing neutralizing antibodies remains unresolved.
Completion criteria require indication-specific numerical endpoints, follow-up durations and safety power calculations. The supplied material establishes no consensus values.
The retained 2023 article extraction is truncated in the references, limiting completeness of the supplied source artifact.

brief.title: Lasting immune control aimed at chosen targets
possible: People with autoimmune disease could receive a short treatment that stops their immune system attacking selected parts of their own body. Doctors could choose antigens—the substances an immune response targets—and make the system tolerate them while keeping its protective defenses.
The same capability could provide lasting relief from severe allergies, help people accept transplanted organs, and prevent immune attacks on therapeutic proteins or gene treatments.
why: Many patients depend on continuing treatment that broadly suppresses immunity. Lasting control of selected harmful responses could free them from those drugs while preserving protection against infections and cancer.
Transplants and replacement cells could last longer if immune attacks stopped. Treatments involving proteins or gene delivery could also work better when the immune system tolerates their components.

sources.who: Jessica E. Kenison, Nikolas A. Stevens and Francisco J. Quintana
sources.showed: Their review describes how the immune system restrains harmful responses and surveys treatments designed to induce tolerance to selected targets. Approaches include antigen delivery and engineered immune cells.
sources.cited_for: It explains the biological basis and treatment approaches for lasting tolerance to chosen antigens.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a broadly adaptable treatment that produces lasting, selective tolerance in patients.

sources.who: Farzan Solimani, Masayuki Amagai, Catherine M. Bollard and Aimee S. Payne
sources.showed: Their review reports drug-free remission in small lupus patient series after treatment with engineered immune cells that remove B cells, a type of immune cell. It also surveys more selective cellular treatments.
sources.quote: A systematic review identified 58 individuals with SLE treated with CD19-targeted CAR T cells;
sources.cited_for: It supports the possibility of lasting drug-free remission after a cellular treatment.
sources.not_established: Removing B cells does not establish tolerance to chosen disease antigens, and small patient series leave broader safety and reliability unresolved.

shown: Clinical teams have achieved drug-free remission in eight initial patients with hard-to-treat lupus using engineered immune cells that remove B cells. Some remissions have lasted years. These small series show lasting disease control, but do not establish tolerance to chosen disease antigens.
missing: A reliable treatment must produce lasting tolerance to chosen targets across different diseases after a short course.
Human studies must connect clinical improvement to selective immune control while showing that protective defenses still work.
Treatments must cover the targets sustaining disease, including harmful responses that expand to new targets.
Independent studies and long-term follow-up must establish reproducibility and characterize serious harms.

milestones.label: Short treatment produces years of tolerance across disease classes
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show years of tolerance to chosen antigens after a short course across different disease classes, without ongoing broad immune suppression. This would establish lasting benefit beyond a single disease class.

milestones.label: Immune tests confirm selective control and preserved defenses
milestones.explanation: Functional tests would have to confirm sustained control of selected harmful responses alongside clinical benefit and preserved protective immunity. This would establish that treatment selectively controls the intended responses.

milestones.label: Independent centers reproduce benefits and define limits
milestones.explanation: Independent centers would have to reproduce results across well-described patient groups and report failures, relapses and additional treatment. This would establish where the approach works and where it falls short.

milestones.label: Long-term follow-up measures serious infection and cancer risks
milestones.explanation: A long-term patient registry would have to estimate serious infection and cancer risks with stated statistical precision. This would characterize safety while leaving uncertainty about rare or delayed harms.

uncertain: Which targets and biological measurements can predict lasting tolerance across patients and disease stages remains unresolved.
It remains unclear whether tolerance treatments can control established antibody-producing responses or remove existing antibodies that block therapy.
The clinical thresholds, follow-up periods and study sizes needed to judge success remain unsettled.

page.title: Antigen-specific immune tolerance induction
page.definition: A clinical platform can be retargeted by changing a selected antigen, a molecule recognized by immune cells. A finite treatment course induces lasting unresponsiveness to that target, controls its clinical consequences and preserves protective immunity without maintenance systemic immunosuppression.

goal.need: NIAID's 2019 programme cited millions of Americans affected by autoimmune disease and childhood food allergy. It seeks selective control of harmful responses to self-proteins, allergens and donor tissue while preserving protective immunity and reducing ongoing immunosuppression.

figures.caption: U.S. disease-burden estimates cited by NIAID on 6 December 2019.
figures.note: These populations can overlap. The estimates describe the programme's published rationale.

statements.body: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
statements.quote: Tolerance induction strategies aim to selectively block or prevent deleterious immune responses, while leaving protective immunity intact.
advance the development of immune tolerance strategies in autoimmunity, allergy, and transplantation by conducting high-quality clinical trials with emerging therapeutic agents.
statements.context: The passage states the Network's mission in a clinical review written by its investigators.

completion.title: A retargeted platform induces off-treatment clinical tolerance while preserving protective immunity.
completion.criterion: The same antigen-delivery or cell-engineering method succeeds clinically after changing its specified antigen target. Controlled human studies meet their registered clinical endpoints after treatment withdrawal, demonstrate functional unresponsiveness to the selected antigen and preserve responses to unrelated protective antigens. Treatment duration, off-treatment follow-up, rescue rules and statistical success boundaries come from each indication's protocol. Recipients require no maintenance systemic immunosuppression.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis of NIAID's tolerance definition and the clinical retargeting capability described here.
completion.basis: Searches of NIAID programme calls, ITN clinical papers, FDA clinical-development material, EMA haemophilia guidance, and tolerance roadmaps and target product profiles found no platform-wide completion test, required antigen count or shared off-treatment duration. Application-specific tolerance phenotypes have been reported. Clinical retargeting with concurrent evidence of off-treatment efficacy, antigen specificity and protective immunity supplies the Atlas test.

milestones.title: A selected-antigen treatment suppresses an animal's target immune response after challenge at P < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: A selected-antigen intervention reduces its target immune response after antigen challenge relative to the published controls. Wallace and colleagues used three weekly pretreatments followed by four weekly uricase challenges in mice, with 8 mice per group and P < 0.05 as the significance boundary. Their report, published on 20 December 2023, found lower uricase-specific IgG after mannose-polymer–uricase treatment than after free uricase or saline. The same method suppressed responses to E. coli asparaginase.
milestones.set_by: Wallace and colleagues, published antigen-challenge experiments and statistical analysis. This experimental protocol was written for therapeutic-protein antigens in mice.
milestones.threshold_quote: The threshold for statistical significance was fixed at p < 0.05.

milestones.title: People tolerate a selected-antigen treatment without serious adverse events through a 3-month safety gate.
milestones.criterion: A first-in-human dose cohort completes its protocol's observation period without the serious adverse events that would prevent escalation. NCT02283671 used cohorts of 3 and a 3-month gate. The study, published on 8 April 2019, treated 12 people, 8 with multiple sclerosis and 4 with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, with peptide-loaded tolerogenic dendritic cells. All 12 completed 24-week safety follow-up. The article reports no serious adverse events and lists possibly related mild events in its adverse-event table.
milestones.set_by: Hospital Clinic of Barcelona investigators, registered protocol NCT02283671 and its published study design. The 3-month escalation gate was written for autoimmune neurological disease.
milestones.threshold_quote: absence of serious adverse events in that previous dose after 3 mo of follow-up.

milestones.title: A selected-antigen treatment reduces its human target response versus placebo at two-sided P < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: A controlled human study meets its prespecified target-antigen immune-response endpoint. TAK-101's coeliac-disease protocol tested the change in gliadin-specific interferon-γ responses on gluten-challenge day 6 at a two-sided significance level of 0.05. The report published on 17 March 2021 randomized 34 people, of whom 33 completed the challenge. Two 8 mg/kg infusions produced an 88% smaller mean response increase than placebo, P = 0.006. The between-group intestinal-histology comparison had P = 0.08.
milestones.set_by: TAK-101 Study Group, registered protocol NCT03738475, described in Kelly and colleagues' paper and supplementary statistical methods. This endpoint was written for coeliac disease.

milestones.title: A selected-antigen treatment meets a clinical efficacy endpoint after maintenance treatment is withdrawn.
milestones.criterion: Achieve superior clinical control at the protocol's assessment after maintenance-treatment withdrawal. GRASS compared nasal symptoms over 0–10 hours after grass challenge 1 year after stopping 2 years of treatment, adjusting for baseline and using two-sided P < 0.05. Its 106-person report on 14 February 2017 failed the primary endpoint, P = 0.75. In a kidney study published on 6 February 2025, 15 of 20 MDR-101 recipients met the >2-year immunosuppression-free endpoint, with 10 standard-care controls. Donors were siblings matched for both HLA tissue-type haplotypes.
milestones.set_by: Immune Tolerance Network GRASS Study Team, registered protocol NCT01335139. Its withdrawal schedule and nasal-challenge endpoint were written for grass-pollen allergy. The kidney result uses the separate MDR-101-MLK protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome was TNSS comparing sublingual immunotherapy vs placebo at year 3.

not_found: No published common numerical milestone sequence covering all four applications was located, so the milestones retain explicitly identified application-specific protocol tests.
Searches did not identify a human platform-retargeting study jointly demonstrating off-treatment clinical efficacy and functional preservation of unrelated protective responses.
ClinicalTrials.gov study-record text was inaccessible for NCT01335139, NCT03738475 and NCT03363945.
The supplied PMC review pages returned browser-verification screens, while their publisher abstracts were accessible.
The MDR-101 publisher full text was inaccessible, while the authors' institutional abstract was accessible.
